analysis.one_liner: Bars federal contracts to offshore tax-haven companies and lawbreaking contractors, and moves government work back in-house.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 2008 with no cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing or vote and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have tightened the rules for companies that win federal contracts. It would have barred federal contracts and grants to companies set up in offshore secrecy havens to avoid U.S. taxes, banned contracting with companies that failed to certify their financial reports, and required every agency to check that a bidder has a decent record of obeying tax, labor, environmental, and consumer protection laws. It also would have required conflict-of-interest safeguards on large contracts, linked bonus fees to actual results, posted more contract details on USASpending.gov, and directed the Defense and Homeland Security departments to shift work that is inherently governmental back to government employees over three years.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who fund roughly hundreds of billions of dollars in federal contracting each year and would get stronger assurance that contractors pay their taxes, obey the law, and actually perform the work they are paid for. Federal employees would also benefit where work now done by contractors is moved back in-house.

how_it_helps.text: Bars award of federal contracts and grants to companies the IRS determines were purposefully organized in an offshore secrecy jurisdiction to avoid federal taxes, with an initial list covering 34 jurisdictions such as the Cayman Islands, Bermuda, Switzerland, and Luxembourg.

Prohibits contracting with publicly traded companies that failed to certify their most recent financial report under Sarbanes-Oxley, with waivers only for national security or minor technical infractions that must be posted publicly.

Requires contracting officers to find that a prospective contractor has a satisfactory record of integrity and business ethics, including compliance with tax, labor, employment, environmental, antitrust, and consumer protection laws, giving the most weight to violations adjudicated in the last five years.

Requires conflicts-of-interest clauses in covered contracts over $500,000 for functions closely associated with government work, including employee financial disclosure, gift bans, and bans on using non-public government information for personal gain.
Bars agencies from paying award fees or bonuses to contractors for work they did not perform or performed poorly, and requires fees to be linked to cost, schedule, and performance outcomes.

Requires the Defense and Homeland Security departments to report which inherently governmental functions are being performed by contractors, and to staff at least 50 percent of those functions with federal employees within one year and 100 percent within two years.

Creates a database for contracting officers of contractors' past defaults, suspensions, debarments, and legal judgments, and adds new disclosures to USASpending.gov, including award fees justifications, the price range of competing bids, and the performance ratings of the top 100 contractors.

analysis.who_pays: Federal contractors, especially defense and homeland security firms and companies organized in offshore tax havens, which would face new eligibility screens, disclosure requirements, the loss of automatic bonus fees, and the possible loss of work that gets brought back in-house.

drawbacks.text: Companies organized abroad, even legitimately, could be swept up by the offshore list, which initially names jurisdictions including Hong Kong, Singapore, and Switzerland, and the determination of whether a company was 'purposefully organized' there to avoid taxes rests on judgment calls by the Treasury Department.

New integrity determinations, conflict-of-interest clauses, and disclosure requirements add paperwork and delay to the contracting process, and the bill's own waivers for national security and emergency contracting show that lawmakers recognized the screens could interfere with urgent needs.

Bringing inherently governmental functions back to federal employees would raise agencies' permanent staffing costs, a trade-off supporters considered worth making but which does not show up in the bill's accounting.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is straightforward: contractors doing the public's work would have to pay their taxes, obey the law, and earn their bonuses. The main costs are administrative burden and some risk that blunt tools, like the offshore list, would catch companies that are not really tax avoiders. On balance the trade-offs modestly favor taxpayers, though the effectiveness of the offshore screen depends heavily on how Treasury writes the rules.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Hillary Clinton introduced the bill in the Senate on June 16, 2008, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.
The committee took no further action on the bill, and there was no markup, floor vote, or House action before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Defense and homeland security contractors and companies organized in offshore tax havens kept the existing rules, with no new eligibility screens, no requirement to bring government work back in-house, and no tighter limits on award fees.

for.name: Hillary Clinton
for.role: U.S. Senator from New York (bill sponsor)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; no senator joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on June 16, 2008 and took no further action; no hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: Joe Lieberman
against.role: Chair, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration during the remainder of the 110th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no senator cosponsored the bill, so the record shows no split, and the visible fact is that no senator of either party signed on.

industries.note: The bill would require these firms' departments to move inherently governmental functions back to federal employees within three years, and would bar paying award fees for unperformed or poorly rated work. Contractors have an interest in keeping that work and those fees, which comes at taxpayers' expense.

industries.industry: Companies organized in offshore secrecy jurisdictions
industries.note: The bill would make companies the IRS finds were organized in offshore havens to avoid federal taxes ineligible for federal contracts and grants. Their offshore structure exists to reduce their U.S. tax bill, which shifts the tax burden to everyone else.

industries.industry: Federal contractors with poor compliance records
industries.note: The bill would require a satisfactory integrity and business ethics record, weigh recent adjudicated violations of tax, labor, environmental, and consumer protection laws against bidders, and stop paying bonuses to low performers. Firms with clean records would gain a competitive edge; firms with violations would lose contracts.

industries.industry: Publicly traded contractors without Sarbanes-Oxley certifications
industries.note: The bill would bar agencies from contracting with public companies that failed to certify their most recent financial report, with a public list of such companies. Investors and taxpayers rely on those certifications for accurate financials.
